analysis.one_liner: Hands federal land energy leasing to states, bypassing environmental and endangered species review.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it died in the Senate Energy Committee at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any state with its own oil and gas rules take over leasing and permitting for energy development on federal land within its borders — land owned by all Americans. Once a state took over, its decisions would no longer count as federal actions, so reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and federal administrative law would no longer apply. Federal royalties would still be collected, and states could keep their own processing fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies seeking to drill on federal land. They would deal with state regulators instead of federal agencies, and state decisions could not be challenged under the federal environmental review, endangered species, or administrative procedure laws that apply today. States that want more drilling would also gain control and could keep application processing fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: A state with an established leasing program could declare that it is taking over leasing, permitting, and regulation of oil, gas, and other energy development on federal land in the state, in place of the federal government.

State actions to lease, permit, or regulate drilling would be exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, the Endangered Species Act of 1973, and the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 — removing the main federal checks, public comment processes, and avenues for judicial review that currently apply.
States could collect and retain lease or permit application processing fees from applicants.
Federal royalties and revenues would still be collected and deposited in federal accounts, so the Treasury would not lose royalty money.

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which owns the federal land. National Parks, wildlife refuges, wilderness areas, and tribal trust lands are excluded, but everything else — roughly 113 million acres of onshore federal land already open, plus land currently off-limits — could be opened by state decision alone. The public would lose the environmental reviews, endangered species protections, public participation, and court challenges that federal law currently provides before drilling proceeds on shared land.

drawbacks.text: State drilling decisions would escape the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act entirely, so impacts on air, water, and wildlife on land owned by all Americans would not have to be studied, disclosed, or mitigated before drilling begins.

Because state actions would not be federal actions, affected citizens and conservation groups would lose the administrative procedures and judicial review routes that the Administrative Procedure Act provides for challenging federal permitting decisions.

States, whose budgets benefit from drilling activity and severance revenues, would act as both regulator and revenue beneficiary over land they do not own, replacing a trustee (the federal government) with an interested party.

The bill's exclusions protect parks, refuges, wilderness, and tribal lands, but every other federal land category would be eligible, including large tracts managed by the Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers faster permitting — the sponsor cites 197 days to process federal drill permits in 2013 — and promises no loss of federal royalties. But the cost side is structural: it removes the environmental review, endangered species safeguards, and court access that federal law applies to drilling on land owned by the whole public, and hands the decision to state governments that directly profit from drilling. For anyone who values those protections on shared land, the trade is a poor one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2017 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator James Inhofe introduced the bill on February 7, 2017, joined by five original Republican cosponsors; eight Republicans cosponsored in total.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that same day.
No committee action, floor action, or vote followed; the last entry in the action history is the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal environmental and endangered species protections on federal land remain intact, since the transfer of authority never happened. Supporters of more drilling gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Environmental safeguards on federal land stayed intact

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to transfer federal land energy leasing to the states and exempt state decisions from NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship came from Republicans — eight senators, all R — with no Democratic or independent support recorded, and the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production
industries.note: Drillers would gain access to federal land permitted by state regulators, with no federal environmental review, no endangered species consultation, and no federal administrative or judicial challenge to state decisions. The savings in time and litigation are borne by the public in unchecked impacts on shared land.
The public's ability to study, comment on, and challenge drilling decisions on federal land would disappear, leaving state-level processes as the only recourse.
